title: Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)

teacherSummary.text: Creon arrives with smooth words. When Oedipus refuses him, Creon reveals that his men have seized Ismene and drags off Antigone. Theseus arrives, rebukes Creon for breaking Athenian law, and sends men to rescue the girls. Creon calls Oedipus polluted; Oedipus answers that he acted unknowingly.

The debate has defined the standard; the close turns it into action still in motion, not a finished rescue. “Enough of words; the captors speed amain, / While we the victims stand debating here” (lines 1065–1066). Theseus then goes with Creon and warns, “One man doth not prevail against the State” (line 1082). The seizure began as a private show of power in the grove; it ends, for this episode, with the city moving to recover the maidens and with the king's refusal to let one captor outtalk or outrun the law. The restoration itself remains a purpose, not yet a reported fact.

anchorPassages.text:
O front of brass, thy subtle tongue would twist
To thy advantage every plea of right
Why try thy arts on me, why spread again
Toils where ’twould gall me sorest to be snared?
In old days when by self-wrought woes distraught,
I yearned for exile as a glad release,
Thy will refused the favour then I craved.
But when my frenzied grief had spent its force,
And I was fain to taste the sweets of home,
Then thou would’st thrust me from my country, then
These ties of kindred were by thee ignored;
And now again when thou behold’st this State
And all its kindly people welcome me,
Thou seek’st to part us, wrapping in soft words
Hard thoughts. And yet what pleasure canst thou find
In forcing friendship on unwilling foes?
Suppose a man refused to grant some boon
When you importuned him, and afterwards
When you had got your heart’s desire, consented,
Granting a grace from which all grace had fled,
Would not such favour seem an empty boon?
Yet such the boon thou profferest now to me,
Fair in appearance, but when tested false.

One of thy daughters is already seized,
The other I will carry off anon.
Woe, woe!
This is but prelude to thy woes.
Hast thou my child?
And soon shall have the other.
Ho, friends! ye will not surely play me false?
Chase this ungodly villain from your land.
Hence, stranger, hence avaunt! Thou doest wrong
In this, and wrong in all that thou hast done.
’Tis time by force to carry off the girl,
If she refuse of her free will to go.
Ah, woe is me! where shall I fly, where find
Succour from gods or men?

Sir, thou dost wrong.

I take but what is mine.

Ho! hasten to the altars, one of you,
Command my liegemen leave the sacrifice
And hurry, foot and horse, with rein unchecked,
To where the paths that packmen use diverge,
Lest the two maidens slip away, and I
Become a mockery to this my guest,
As one despoiled by force. Quick, as I bid.
As for this stranger, had I let my rage,
Justly provoked, have play, he had not ’scaped
Scathless and uncorrected at my hands.
But now the laws to which himself appealed,
These and none other shall adjudicate.
Thou shalt not quit this land, till thou hast fetched
The maidens and produced them in my sight.
Thou hast offended both against myself
And thine own race and country. Having come
Unto a State that champions right and asks
For every action warranty of law,
Thou hast set aside the custom of the land,
And like some freebooter art carrying off
What plunder pleases thee, as if forsooth
Thou thoughtest this a city without men,
Or manned by slaves, and me a thing of naught.

anchorPassages.text:
O shameless railer, think’st thou this abuse
Defames my grey hairs rather than thine own?
Murder and incest, deeds of horror, all
Thou blurtest forth against me, all I have borne,
No willing sinner; so it pleased the gods
Wrath haply with my sinful race of old,
Since thou could’st find no sin in me myself
For which in retribution I was doomed
To trespass thus against myself and mine.
Answer me now, if by some oracle
My sire was destined to a bloody end
By a son’s hand, can this reflect on me,
Me then unborn, begotten by no sire,
Conceivèd in no mother’s womb? And if
When born to misery, as born I was,
I met my sire, not knowing whom I met
Or what I did, and slew him, how canst thou
With justice blame the all-unconscious hand?

questions.expected: “Command”, “minions” and “slave” stand out. “Command your minions” tells Theseus to give orders only to his own servants, and “I am not your slave” refuses Athenian authority in one insult. Creon rejects the host city’s command and will not be treated as its slave (Creon, line 869).

questions.q: How does this line connect to refuge and hospitality?
questions.expected: Creon refuses the host city’s authority and will not be treated as its slave; the line shows the seizure of the daughters as a rejection of Athenian hospitality and law.

items.text: What does Theseus say Athens asks of every action, in lines 956–958?
items.lookFor: He says Athens is “a State that champions right and asks / For every action warranty of law.” The line is the standard he holds Creon to: having entered such a city, Creon has “set aside the custom of the land, / And like some freebooter” carried off what he pleased. The demand is not courtesy; it is the legal condition on which a stranger may act inside Athens.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He says Athens is “a State that champions right and asks / For every action warranty of law.” The line is the standard he holds Creon to: having entered such a city, Creon has “set aside the custom of the land, / And like some freebooter” carried off what he pleased. The demand is not courtesy; it is the legal condition on which a stranger may act inside Athens.

items.text: What does Creon reveal he has already done before he has Antigone seized on stage?
items.lookFor: He tells Oedipus that “One of thy daughters is already seized, / The other I will carry off anon.” Ismene is already in his men's hands, offstage, and the visible struggle over Antigone is only “prelude to thy woes.” The revelation shows that the turn from persuasion to force began before this confrontation, not in a sudden moment of anger alone.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

items.text: Why does Creon pretend friendship at first?
items.lookFor: He hopes to persuade Oedipus to return before he has to use force, and he wants the chorus to see him as a kinsman, not a raider. He arrives saying, “I come with no ill purpose; I am old,” claims he was “chosen to persuade your guest and bring / Him back to Thebes,” and appeals to pity for Antigone’s hardship. Only after Oedipus refuses—“leave me here; whate’er may be my lot”—does he show that a daughter is already seized. The courtesy is a tactic, not a change of aim.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: He hopes to persuade Oedipus to return before he has to use force, and he wants the chorus to see him as a kinsman, not a raider. He arrives saying, “I come with no ill purpose; I am old,” claims he was “chosen to persuade your guest and bring / Him back to Thebes,” and appeals to pity for Antigone’s hardship. Only after Oedipus refuses—“leave me here; whate’er may be my lot”—does he show that a daughter is already seized. The courtesy is a tactic, not a change of aim.

items.text: Why does Theseus refuse to let his just anger decide Creon's punishment on the spot?
items.lookFor: He will use the same laws Creon himself appealed to, not a private revenge. “But now the laws to which himself appealed, / These and none other shall adjudicate,” he says, and he will not let Creon leave “till thou hast fetched / The maidens and produced them in my sight.” The choice keeps Athens from becoming the lawless city Creon has treated it as, even while Theseus admits that his rage was “Justly provoked” (line 949).
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: He will use the same laws Creon himself appealed to, not a private revenge. “But now the laws to which himself appealed, / These and none other shall adjudicate,” he says, and he will not let Creon leave “till thou hast fetched / The maidens and produced them in my sight.” The choice keeps Athens from becoming the lawless city Creon has treated it as, even while Theseus admits that his rage was “Justly provoked” (line 949).

items.text: What does “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” suggest about Creon seizes the daughters? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: An inference that Creon’s persuasion was cover for force: when words fail he takes hostages, which shows that Thebes wants control of Oedipus, not his welfare.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: When Oedipus refuses him, Creon reveals, “One of thy daughters is already seized, / The other I will carry off anon” (lines 840–841). The seizure was planned before the persuasion ended, so the kind words were never the real plan. He treats the daughters as leverage, “those two crutches” (line 883), because what he wants is control of Oedipus himself.

items.text: Find one example of conflict in “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”. What does it reveal about Creon seizes the daughters that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A specific clash, such as the rapid “wrong” / “right” exchange, explained for what it shows: Creon claims a right over his kin while using force.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: In the exchange “Sir, thou dost wrong. / Nay, right. / How right? / I take but what is mine.” (lines 857–860), Creon claims ownership of Antigone as her kinsman while his men drag her away. The conflict shows him dressing force in the language of rights, which a plain statement about a kidnapping would miss.

items.text: How does the characterization in “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” shape what we understand about Creon seizes the daughters?
items.lookFor: How Creon is drawn as smooth, then menacing, and Theseus as angry but restrained, so the seizure reads as a clash between two kinds of power.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Creon opens gently (“I come with no ill purpose; I am old,” line 750) and ends with “Nothing shall curb my will” (line 913). Oedipus names the pattern: “wrapping in soft words / Hard thoughts” (lines 792–793). Theseus admits his rage was “Justly provoked” (line 949) yet holds it back. The characterization makes the seizure a test of two kinds of power: a ruler who restrains himself and an envoy who does not.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Burghers, my noble friends…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from Creon’s opening speech (lines 747–778) with their connotations, such as “noble friends,” “kinsman,” “foster-mother” or “Hide it,” showing flattery and family language used to persuade.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Creon calls the elders “my noble friends” (line 747) and Thebes Oedipus’s “old foster-mother” (line 778). Both are warm words of friendship and family. They flatter the hosts and make leaving Athens sound like going home to a mother, hiding Thebes’ plan to keep him outside its borders.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn comes when persuasion fails: Oedipus exposes Creon’s real purpose and Creon reveals the seizure. The effect is open force, the elders’ call to arms, and Theseus’s arrival.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn is caused by Oedipus exposing Creon’s aim: “Thou art come to take me, not to take me home, / But plant me on thy borders” (lines 803–804). With persuasion gone, Creon turns to force and reveals that a daughter is already taken (line 840). The effect is open conflict that the elders cannot stop, so they call for help (“Men of Athens, arm ye, arm!”, line 928) and Theseus must answer.

items.text: How does “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” build on “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A cause-and-effect link: the ode praised Athens as able to defend its guest, and Antigone’s first line calls on the land to make that praise good, so Episode 2 tests the ode.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode ended by praising Athens’ strength. Antigone’s first words turn the praise into a challenge: “O land extolled above all lands, ’tis now / For thee to make these glorious titles good” (lines 740–741). The ode sets up the test: having boasted, the land must now prove it can defend its guest against Creon.

items.text: In “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about Creon seizes the daughters, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: Creon claims grief and kinship, but his motive is political control of Oedipus; even his appeal to Athens’ court is an excuse after the force.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Creon claims to come from grief: “of all Thebans I have most bewailed, / Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes” (lines 757–758). His actions show another motive: he has already taken one daughter and threatens to “Carry off this man” (line 897). Afterwards he says he trusted Athens’ court, which “permits not vagrant folk / To stay within your borders” (lines 995–996). He reaches for any argument that excuses getting Oedipus back under Thebes’ control.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (How can you tell when someone is pretending to care in order to control you?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer that uses Oedipus’s test of Creon, a favour offered only when it serves the giver, or the gap between Creon’s tears and his seizure.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: I first said you can tell by tone of voice. Oedipus gives a better test: timing. A favour offered after it was refused when you needed it is “Fair in appearance, but when tested false” (line 801). Creon offered a home only once Oedipus became useful, and when refused he turned to force. Care that becomes force when it is declined was control all along.

items.text: Does intent decide guilt? Evaluate Oedipus' argument in lines 1019–1023, using evidence from this scene.
items.lookFor: An evaluation of Oedipus’s argument that he cannot be blamed for killing a father he did not know, weighed against other evidence in the play (he calls the acts horrors; he must live with them), with a position and a counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: intent decides moral guilt, but not every consequence. Oedipus says he “met my sire, not knowing whom I met / Or what I did” (lines 1021–1022) and asks how Creon can “blame the all-unconscious hand” (line 1023). His example of a man turning on an attacker (lines 1040–1045) is persuasive. Counter-line: he still calls the acts “deeds of horror” (line 1008) and has lived with them, so the play separates blame from suffering rather than erasing the deed.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The rule of law against force: Theseus defends Athens as a state "that champions right" (line 957). How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines: Theseus hands Creon to the laws he appealed to and condemns him for setting aside custom; a qualification that Theseus also uses force, but lawful force.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. Theseus will not punish Creon in rage; he condemns him for having “set aside the custom of the land” (line 959) and acting “like some freebooter” (line 960). The qualification is that Theseus also uses force, sending “foot and horse” after the captors (line 943). The scene does not oppose law to all force; it opposes lawful force to lawless seizure.

items.text: Which character in “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” acts most wisely in the matter of Creon seizes the daughters, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard, such as restraint under provocation, applied to Theseus and Creon (or the elders), with a line for each.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of restraint, Theseus acts most wisely. His rage was “Justly provoked” (line 949), but he hands Creon to the law and first sends men after the maidens: “Quick, as I bid” (line 947). By the same standard Creon acts least wisely, boasting “Nothing shall curb my will” (line 913) in a foreign city. A student could also rank the elders highly for standing up to Creon unarmed: “Restore the maidens, else thou goest not” (line 893).

items.text: You are directing “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of Creon seizes the daughters.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as father and daughter reaching for each other, Theseus’s entrance cutting through the noise, or Oedipus’s curse, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) On “Thy hands, my child! / They will not let me, father” (lines 879–880), keep Oedipus and Antigone reaching toward each other with a guard’s arm between them, a gap of a few feet the blind man cannot cross. The audience feels the cruelty without seeing violence. (2) Let Theseus enter at a run and stop the noise with one line, “Why this outcry? What is forward?” (line 931), standing still while everyone else moves. His calm shows the authority that will judge the seizure.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 740–1091: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Where was Theseus when the outcry called him? (At the altar of Poseidon, line 932.) Why/how: How does Creon justify the seizure? (He takes “what is mine,” line 860, and later cites Athens’ court, lines 993–996.) Should/what if: Should Theseus have punished Creon on the spot? (Answers weigh his justified anger, line 949, against his choice of law, lines 951–952.)

items.text: Connect “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”, with its focus on Creon seizes the daughters, to refuge and hospitality: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about refuge and hospitality, the question’s theme. Creon violates both by seizing suppliants and guests of Athens, and Theseus defends them. A strong answer says what must still be proved.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong. Creon’s crime is a crime against hospitality: Theseus accuses him of “Haling by force their suppliants, poor maids” (line 968), and Oedipus says Athens is “the land whence thou wast fain to steal / Their aged suppliant” (lines 1057–1058). But the link is still a promise. Theseus swears that “nothing save my death / Will stay my purpose to restore the maids” (lines 1088–1089). To strengthen it, Sophocles must show whether the host can keep that oath.

items.text: Is the conflict in “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” effective in presenting Creon seizes the daughters, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion, such as whether the conflict develops through argument as well as action, with one line that meets it and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because the conflict is fought with arguments as well as hands. After the seizure comes a real trial of words: Oedipus asks whether Creon, if attacked, “Would’st thou, O man of justice, first inquire / If the assassin was perchance thy sire” (lines 1041–1042). Counter-line: the quick insults “Insolence! / Insolence that thou must bear” (lines 925–926) may feel melodramatic. A reviewer could call that stretch heavy-handed, though it shows how fast order collapses.

items.text: Compare how “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” treats Creon seizes the daughters with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (a story of a government or family forcing an exile home) and one thing the episode sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: News stories about governments demanding that exiles be handed back usually frame it as politics. Episode 2 sees the personal cruelty inside the politics: Creon calls Antigone and Ismene “those two crutches” (line 883), using the daughters a blind father leans on as leverage. The play shows how a political claim can be enforced by attacking the most private bonds.

items.text: Predict what “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, Theseus’s riders sent after the captors and his oath to bring back the maids, about what the elders will sing while they wait, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: Theseus has sent riders “To where the paths that packmen use diverge” (line 944), so a chase is under way offstage. Clue 2: he swears that nothing but his death will stop him (lines 1088–1089). Left behind with Oedipus, the elders will probably imagine the chase and pray for its outcome. After reading, students check whether the ode stays hopeful or turns to fear.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about Creon seizes the daughters?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a powerful relative uses friendly persuasion, then force against dependants, to reclaim someone protected elsewhere, and a host answers with law. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: A wealthy uncle visits a shelter, all concern and tears, to bring his estranged blind brother home. Refused, he has his men put the brother’s two caregivers into a car, and the shelter director calls the police and detains the uncle until they are brought back. Two things must stay: the switch from “soft words” (line 792) to force, and the host’s insistence that the law, not revenge, will judge (lines 951–952).
